paper_title: Self-Improvement with Auxiliary Rewards: Learning from Verified Traces and Evaluating Transfer

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Answer-level rewards cannot distinguish reasoning traces with equally correct outcomes. We study whether auxiliary trajectory preferences improve small-language-model self-improvement and transfer under limited supervision. We compare confidence-based (SC) and entropy-based metrics (UID-Conj.), which combines global entropy variation and local smoothness, through online reward augmentation and offline training on correct responses. Online experiments adapt Qwen3-1.7B on 30 AIME problems without reference answers; offline experiments use historical AIME problems. UID-Conj. improves the online macro-average across the adaptation benchmark and three transfer benchmarks by 2.08 percentage points over unmodified TTRL. The strongest evidence comes from offline weighted SFT: UID-Conj. exceeds uniform weighting on the same response pool by 1.93 points, with a paired prompt-bootstrap 95\% CI of [0.44, 3.44]. Benefits are task-dependent: SC rewards judged trace quality and instruction following, while UID-Conj. rewards yield stronger training outcomes in several settings. We find that auxiliary preferences can expose learning value among equally correct traces not captured during inference time, motivating their evaluation through downstream gains.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Recent advances in reasoning post-training have strengthened small language models (Yang et al., 2025; Guo et al., 2025), but further improvement under limited supervision requires making better use of available training problems. Selfimprovement offers one route: models generate reasoning traces and learn from feedback on their own responses (Zelikman et al., 2022; Haluptzok et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2024). Answer-level feedback, such as the checkable outcomes used in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) (Guo 1 Figure 1: Correct answers leave room for preference. We investigate whether these trajectory preferences improve learning and downstream transfer. et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025), provides practical training signal but cannot distinguish responses with equally correct final answers. Such responses may differ in the soundness of their reasoning, the completeness of their justification, and the amount of unnecessary repetition; they may also differ in their value as training examples. Auxiliary preferences over these traces could provide additional supervision without requiring new problems or step-level annotations. We therefore ask: when answer-level rewards cannot distinguish successful solutions, can auxiliary trajectory preferences improve learning and downstream transfer? We investigate two auxiliary signals derived from the models own predictive token distributions. Self-Certainty (SC) (Kang et al., 2025) favors trajectories with greater predictive confidence. The second signal, inspired by uniform information density (UID) (Meister et al., 2021), favors trajectories that combine global entropy variation with local smoothness, following observations of locally smooth but globally non-uniform information flow in successful reasoning (Gwak et al., 2026). These signals define alternative preferences among responses receiving the same answer-level reward. The central hypothesis of our study is that auxiliary preferences provide useful learning signals beyond answer-level feedback, improving task performance under limited supervision. To test this hypothesis, we compare training with and without auxiliary preferences while retaining the underlying answer-level supervision. Specifically, we adopt test-time reinforcement learning (TTRL) (Zuo et al., 2026) for only 2 epoch of training to adapt the model on small set test time without reference answers, therefore using only 30 AIME2026 problems. Within TTRL, we augment majority-agreement rewards with auxiliary preferences among responses supporting the majority answer, preserving the reward between agreeing and disagreeing responses. Results show that auxiliary trajectory preferences can improve self-improvement from answerlevel feedback. After adaptation on just 30 AIME2026 problems without reference answers, TTRL augmented with Self Certainty and UID Conjunction metric (UID-Conj.) improve Qwen31.7Bs macro-average accuracy across four mathematics and science benchmarks by 2.03 and 2.08 percentage points, respectively. The benefits extend to critique-verdict prediction and evidenceconditioned scientific reasoning. UID-Conj. improves CriticBench verdict accuracy by 1.24 points, incorrect-class F1 by 1.58 points, and LabBench2 accuracy by 0.76 points, without task-specific training. Complementary offline extensions show that UID-Conj. also improves Qwen3-1.7Bs macroaverage by 1.25 points over random correctcorrect DPO preferences and by 1.93 points over uniform SFT. To summarize, our contributions are: An independent assessment of whether auxiliary signals distinguish reasoning quality among correct responses. controlled study of auxiliary trajectory preferences for small-model self-improvement with limited training data, spanning online and offline settings with controls matched within each objective. An evaluation of transfer from mathematical self-improvement to critique and researchlevel reasoning.

These findings leave two questions unresolved: whether the scores identify useful differences among already-correct responses, and whether reinforcing those improves generation. Self-improvement with outcome, process, and internal feedback. Self-improvement methods use feedback on model-generated responses to refine reasoning. STaR learns from its own rationales that yield correct answers (Zelikman et al., 2022), while DeepSeek models use RL with outcome feedback (Shao et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025). Process supervision provides finer-grained feedback on intermediate steps (Lightman et al., 2023), while there have been research on preferring answers by length (Arora and Zanette, 2025). Closest to ours, Intuitor uses SC as the sole reward in GRPO and reports generalization from mathematics to out-ofdomain tasks (Zhao et al., 2026), and Agarwal et al. (2025) minimizes entropy during training. This establishes internal confidence as self-improvement signal and raises specific question: does entropytrajectory structure add useful supervision beyond confidence when correctness feedback is available? Transfer beyond verifiable training tasks. Math datasets with known answers provide accessible supervision for reasoning models (Hendrycks et al., 2021; Shao et al., 2024), but the intended applications may exceed this supervision in both difficulty and scope. Easy-to-hard generalization studies whether supervision from simpler problems can support harder math reasoning (Sun et al., 2024), while scientific question answering exposes the difficulty of evaluating outputs that require specialized expertise (Rein et al., 2023). Open research problems often lack gold answers for outcomebased rewards, even when proposed solutions can be checked. This gap motivates testing both transfer to harder math and transfer beyond verified answer generation. Best-of-N selection. Selection methods exploit different properties of sampled reasoning. Selfconsistency aggregates agreement across final answers (Wang et al., 2023), whereas Self-Certainty (SC) scores responses using statistics of predictive distributions (Kang et al., 2025). sections.title: 3.1 Experiment Setup
sections.content: Models and rollout configurations. We evaluate fixed Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B checkpoints with thinking enabled, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, and response and context limits of 8,192 and 16,384 tokens, respectively. We sample eight responses per prompt and evaluate all selectors on identical nested pools of size {2, 4, 8}. Datasets and prompts. We use AIME2026, HMMT2026, and MinervaMath, for both inferencetime analyses. See Appendix for prompts. Selection methods. We compare three selectors that directly selects among the rollout batch: Majority Voting, which selects the most frequent final answer. Self-Certainty (SC), which selects the response with the highest confidence-based score, UID-Conj, which selects the response with the highest product of two calibrated global and local scores, favoring responses that score highly on both. See Appendix A.1 for how each selector is calculated. sections.content: The modest accuracy gains in Section 3.2 do not substantially establish the effectiveness of the auxiliary scores. Also, it lacks qualitative analysis on when which signal is more useful than the other. We therefore compare trace quality while holding final-answer correctness fixed. From each eligible candidate pool, we select verifier-correct responses using SC, UID-Conj, and random correct selection, then have judge independently assess their validity, sufficiency, consistency, and relevance/nonredundancy without access to selector identity or reference answer. sections.title: 5 Experiment
sections.content: 5.1 Experiment Setup Models, training data, and benchmarks. We use Qwen3-1.7B as base model, and additionally test on Qwen3-4B as well. Trainings are done for only 2 epochs for RL and 1 epoch for offline training. For online training, we perform test-time adaptation on AIME2026 without reference answers. For offline extensions, we use historical AIME problems gathered until 2025. We evaluate mathematical reasoning on AIME2026, HMMT2026, and MinervaMath, and science reasoning on GPQAs Diamond subset for verifiable tasks, and use CriticBench and LabBench2 for research-level reasoning. We also further evaluate on instruction following tasks to explore the different effects of different auxiliary rewards. Comparison methods. We compare UID-Conj. and SC within each training objective. Online comparisons include the base model, original TTRL, and random auxiliary-score control. For DPO, we compare auxiliary-score preferences against randomly selected and oriented correct vs. correct pairs. For weighted SFT, uniform weighting provides the control on the same correct response pool. Evaluation. For verifiable mathematical benchmarks, we report mean accuracy across five sampled responses per question. For CriticBench, we report verdict accuracy and incorrect-class F1, which assess verdict correctness rather than critique quality. For IFBench, we report prompt-level loose accuracy using the official verifiers. For IHEval, we use the official task-specific metrics and aggregation procedure, reporting results separately for reference, aligned, and conflicting instruction settings. We document dataset sizes, subset selection, decoding configurations, and training hyperparameters in Appendix C. sections.title: 6 Further Analyses
sections.content: Uncertainty Analysis. We report 95% paired prompt-cluster bootstrap confidence intervals for performance differences, retaining all five responses within each resampled prompt. The primary multi-benchmark estimates weight benchmarks equally. The online gains of UID-Conj over TTRL and Random-TTRL have intervals that include zero, as does the offline DPO comparison. The offline weighted-SFT comparison has positive interval, as do the CriticBench accuracy and F1 comparisons against TTRL. However, the CriticBench comparisons against Random-TTRL and 8 auxiliary terms within majority-agreeing groups would more closely isolate their association with individual trajectories (Appendix B.2.1). In addition, the trace-quality diagnostic currently uses one model judge on verifier-correct responses. Transfer evaluation measures critique-verdict accuracy, evidence-conditioned scientific responses, and programmatically verified instruction following, rather than unrestricted open-ended reasoning. Broader response cohorts and human validation would extend this assessment. In particular, the observed difference between trace-selection quality and training utility motivates developing auxiliary preferences that predict responses contribution to learning.

sections.title: Broader Impact and Ethical Implications
sections.content: Improving compact models from limited training data may make reasoning systems more accessible in settings where larger models or extensive supervision are impractical. Auxiliary signals derived from predictive distributions offer way to reuse model-generated responses without requiring separately trained reward model or step-level training annotations. However, generating and scoring multiple trajectories still incurs computational costs, and our experiments do not establish net energy or cost savings. Self-improvement can also reinforce existing errors: majority agreement may reflect shared misconceptions, while predictive confidence and smooth entropy trajectories do not guarantee factual or logical validity. The observed gains in critique and scientific benchmarks should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of dependable autonomous scientific judgment. Moreover, our ultimate goal is to extend reasoning improvements to tasks where reliable answer-level supervision is unavailable, such as research-level mathematics (Son et al., 2026; Glazer et al., 2024). sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: Correct answers do not exhaust the learning signal in model-generated reasoning. Our results show that auxiliary trajectory preferences can extract additional training value from existing responses under limited supervision, with the clearest evidence coming from UID-Conj-weighted SFT on verifiercorrect traces. They also reveal distinction between judged trace quality and training utility: SC selects higher-rated traces, while UID-Conj yields larger gains in our offline training comparisons and selected transfer tasks. These findings motivate evaluating trajectory preferences by the learning outcomes they support, alongside their ability to identify high-quality reasoning.

Reference answers are retained for evaluation and diagnostics; training rewards are computed from agreement with majority-vote pseudo-labels obtained from model-generated responses. For each prompt, the default configuration generates eight responses for majority voting and uses all eight for training. We compare original TTRL, random-preference control, Self-Certainty (SC), and UID-based preferences. The auxiliary preferences do not determine the majority-vote answer. sections.content: D.1 Performance of Warm-start SFT for DPO training We apply warm-start SFT before DPO to adapt the policy to the target tasks through supervised examples. Comparing this checkpoint with the base model isolates the contribution of SFT and establishes reference for subsequent DPO gains. As shown in Table 10, warm-start SFT improves AIME2026 and MM accuracy by 0.67 and 1.25 percentage points, respectively, but reduces HMMT2026 accuracy by 1.22 points, yielding modest macro-average gain of 0.23 points. Thus, SFT largely preserves baseline accuracy; its benefit as DPO initialization is established through direct comparison of DPO checkpoints in Table 4. D.2 UID-Conj. Metric Analysis. Conjunction Metric Variant: UID-Mix. UIDMix combines global entropy variation and local smoothness with equal weight. In the online implementation, we average token entropies computed from renormalized top-25 probabilities into 32 equal-position bins and normalize the resulting trajectory by its mean. We measure global variation using the population variance of this trajectory and local smoothness using the negative mean absolute difference between adjacent bins. Each feature is mapped to an empirical midrank quantile among eligible responses to the same prompt, yielding qG and qS, and the final score is UID-Mix = 1 2 (qG + qS). Unlike UID-Conj, which multiplies these quantiles, UID-Conj = qGqS, UID-Mix allows higher value on one component to compensate more readily for lower value on the other. Results. The product favors responses ranking highly in both global variation and local smoothness, rather than directly rewarding low entropy throughout. This difference offers possible explanation for UID-Conjs stronger offline results. Once finalanswer correctness is fixed, SC may concentrate training on patterns the model already expresses confidently. UID-Conj can instead emphasize successful traces that move between moreand lesscertain stages while maintaining locally smooth transitions. Together with its diagnostic advantage on relevance/non-redundancy, this suggests that UID-Conj may provide complementary preferences over focused, successful reasoning that confidence-based scoring ranks lower. However, SC measures distributional certainty rather than generated-token likelihood, so high SC does not necessarily imply low training loss or less useful update. The training objectives translate these preferences into different learning emphasis. For two correct responses to the same prompt, weighted SFT assigns wi wj = exp(α(qi qj)) , (24) UID-Conj can therefore favor different successful trajectories without selecting the response with the highest overall judge score. This interpretation is consistent with UID-Conjs higher offline aggregates and CriticBench point estimates. Conversely, reinforcing confidently expressed response patterns may help account for SCs higher instruction-following aggregate. These links remain hypotheses: the equations establish how the preferences differ and enter training, while the mixed online results show that their downstream value depends on the setting. E.2 Further Directions The preceding interpretation motivates examining whether UID-Conjs training benefits arise from preferences that complement predictive certainty, and how this relationship changes with the current policy and training objective. central question is whether entropy-trajectory structure helps identify useful updates among already-correct responses beyond what response length, confidence, and judged quality capture. In the online setting, understanding how these preferences interact with advantage normalization could further clarify when they influence learning. Resolving these questions would inform the design of auxiliary signals that better connect response-level properties with downstream training utility.
